sources.note: The primary description of Waalubal stress that every source in our record (Hayes 1980, Hammond 1986, Goedemans 1998, the StressTyp2 entry for this language) cites; our classification rests on a one-sentence secondary mention plus database-carried sentences, and the sources disagree on whether the peninitial shift is categorical (Hayes) or optional (Hammond) and whether a long vowel beyond the 2nd syllable can take main stress (Cunningham/Sharpe for sister dialects say first long vowel anywhere).

sources.citation: Sharpe, Margaret C. (1998). Dictionary of Yugambeh, including neighbouring dialects. Pacific Linguistics C-139. Canberra: ANU. (already, read now for this record)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p.14: 'Like English, Yugambeh is stress-timed, as are the other dialects of this language ... the first syllable of a word is usually stressed and clear, except when there is a long vowel elsewhere in the word, which then gets the primary stress, and the first syllable is less clear.' p.16: 'Long vowels (all the ones with h written after them) are stressed; otherwise the first syllable of a word is stressed. There are never (or almost never) two long vowels in a row.'

sources.quote: 'A syllable contains as nucleus a vowel with or without length. Stress occurs on the first syllable of the word, or on the first long syllable if such is present. Syllable patterns are of the form CV(:)(C), and words contain from one to five syllables.'
